newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel says forex loans less attractive.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel says forex loans less attractive.

text.p: Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel said on Tuesday that last week's 1.2 percentage point cut in interest rates had reduced the attractiveness of foreign currency-linked loans.

"It could very well be that some of the people who thought it worth while to take loans in foreign currency and invest in shekel (deposits) and receive the high interest rate could now be taking into account that perhaps the interest rate on shekels is a little less high than what it was in the past and perhaps not worthwhile to them," Frenkel told Israel's army radio.

Until last week, the premium that Israeli interest rates had over foreign rates caused many businesses to take loans linked to foreign currency. They then converted these loans into shekels, spurring demand that strengthened the Israeli currency.

Last week the central bank cut its key lending rate 1.2 percentage points to an annual 12.7 percent after the cabinet approved exchange rate reforms which widened the upper limit, but not the lower limit, of the diagonal band in which the shekel may trade.
The changes increased the room for depreciation of the shekel, which had traded at the lower limit of the band for most of the past year.
Speculation leading up to the cabinet's decision focussed on a reform that would have widened both limits, which would have allowed the shekel to appreciate further.

"Everyone thought all the talk about the exchange rate and the widening of the band and all those technical words would in the end lead to an appreciation of the shekel. And we said all along the purpose was not to bring about appreciations or devaluations. The purpose was to enable a better market with risks. What happened in the last couple of days was in line with that," Frenkel said.
"But I don't suggest looking at a day or two, rather at longer range tendencies," he added.
In early Tuesday trading the shekel plunged two percent to 3.55 shekels per dollar. This followed a 1.4 percent decline on Monday.

The sharp depreciation will give the central bank relief from the constant need to intervene in the market to prevent the Israeli currency from appreciating beyond its band. The strength of the shekel until last week had forced the Bank of Israel to buy dollars on a massive scale.
